title: Inter-Service Communication
summary: Synchronous and asynchronous calling patterns between services, how a caller finds a live instance, and why one slow service can take down a whole call chain.

slides.markdown:
Once you've split a system into services (see [service-decomposition](service-decomposition)), they need to talk. There are two fundamentally different ways: **synchronous** — call, wait, get a response — and **asynchronous** — publish an event and move on.

Most real systems use both: synchronous for anything the caller needs an answer to right now, asynchronous for anything that can happen "eventually." Picking wrong in either direction is where microservices reliability problems come from.

**Synchronous** communication means the caller sends a request and blocks — or at least keeps the connection open — until it gets a response. This is what **REST over HTTP** and **gRPC** both give you: Service A calls Service B, waits, and only proceeds once B answers.

It's the natural fit whenever the caller genuinely needs the answer to continue — checkout can't confirm an order until Payments confirms the charge went through. The cost is a direct dependency: if B is slow or down, A is now slow or down too, for exactly as long as A is waiting on it.

That coupling is fine when it matches a real business dependency; it's a liability when it's used just because synchronous calls are the easiest thing to write.

slides.sectionTitle: Asynchronous communication via events and queues
slides.markdown:
**Asynchronous** communication means the caller publishes a message — an event to a broker like Kafka, or a job onto a queue like SQS — and moves on without waiting for anyone to process it. The receiving service consumes it whenever it's ready, possibly seconds or minutes later.

This decouples the caller from the callee's availability and speed entirely: if the Notifications service is down for five minutes, order confirmations still get placed, they just get emailed a bit late once Notifications catches back up. The trade is that the caller no longer gets an immediate answer — you need to design for eventual consistency and figure out how (or whether) to tell the user when something fails downstream.

Good fits: sending a receipt email, updating a search index, recording an analytics event — anything where "a bit later" is fine.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a request fanning out across three services synchronously
slides.markdown:
![Order Service fanning out synchronously to three downstream services](assets/sync-fanout-latency.svg)

One incoming request becomes four network calls, and the total latency is at least the sum of whichever calls can't happen in parallel — often close to the slowest of the three downstream services, not the average.

This is the shape every synchronous fan-out takes: the caller is only as fast, and only as available, as the slowest and least reliable service it waits on.

slides.sectionTitle: Service discovery: how a caller finds a live instance
slides.markdown:
In a horizontally-scaled system, "call the Inventory service" isn't a fixed address — there might be twenty instances of it, starting and stopping as autoscaling and deploys happen. **Service discovery** is the mechanism that answers "which live instance handles this call right now."

Two common shapes: **client-side discovery**, where the caller asks a registry (like Consul or etcd) for a list of healthy instances and picks one itself; and **server-side discovery**, where the caller just calls a stable name and a load balancer or proxy resolves it to a live instance behind the scenes — the more common approach in practice, and the deeper mechanics live in [service-discovery](service-discovery).

Either way, the registry needs a way to know an instance died — usually a health check — or callers keep routing to dead instances.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: sync vs async inter-service communication trade-offs
slides.markdown:
| | Synchronous (REST/gRPC) | Asynchronous (events/queues) |
|---|---|---|
| Caller gets an immediate answer | Yes | No — the result, if any, arrives later |
| Coupling to callee's uptime | Direct — callee down means caller blocked or failing | Decoupled — messages queue up until the consumer recovers |
| Best fit | Caller needs the result to proceed (payment confirmation) | Caller doesn't need to wait (send receipt, update search index) |
| Failure mode | Cascades — one slow service slows its callers | Contained — a backlog grows, but callers keep moving |

**How to decide:** ask whether the calling code has a next step that depends on the answer right now — if yes, synchronous; if the work can happen "a bit later" without the user noticing, make it asynchronous.

slides.sectionTitle: gRPC vs REST between services: why gRPC is common internally
slides.markdown:
| | REST (JSON over HTTP) | gRPC (protobuf over HTTP/2) |
|---|---|---|
| Payload format | JSON — human-readable, larger on the wire | Binary protobuf — smaller, faster to (de)serialize |
| Contract | Loose — often an OpenAPI doc, drifts from code | Strict — a `.proto` schema generates client/server code, catching mismatches at compile time |
| Streaming | Awkward — needs SSE or WebSockets bolted on | Native — bidirectional streaming built into the protocol |
| Typical use | Public/external APIs — wide client compatibility, easy to debug with curl | Internal service-to-service calls — speed and strict contracts matter more than human-readability |

**How to decide:** REST for anything a browser, a partner, or a human with curl needs to call; gRPC for high-volume internal calls between services you control on both ends, where the schema contract and the performance both pay off.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a synchronous call chain that turns one slow service into a full outage
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Each service is independently healthy, so the overall system is healthy."

**Why it's wrong:** if Service A calls B synchronously, and B calls C synchronously, then C running slow — say, a database query that usually takes 20ms now takes 8 seconds — means B's threads sit blocked waiting on C, and A's threads sit blocked waiting on B. Without timeouts, a slowdown in C can exhaust the thread pool or connection pool in every service upstream of it, turning one slow dependency into a total outage across the whole chain.

**Correct model:** every synchronous call needs an explicit timeout and, ideally, a circuit breaker that stops calling a consistently failing dependency — treat "how does this call fail" as part of the design, not an afterthought once it happens in production.
